question.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{3},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{3}=\frac{4}{9}(\frac{27}{64})=\frac{3}{16} \\ {a}_{4} & =\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{4}=\frac{4}{9}(\frac{81}{256})=\frac{9}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(\frac{9}{64})}{(\frac{3}{16})}=\frac{9}{64}\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{16})}{(1-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{16})}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
